fields.Front: Define entity, attribute, value and domain, using the instructor's employee/salary contrast.
fields.Back:
Entity: a single thing with INDEPENDENT EXISTENCE - any object in the mini-world we store information about ('an employee is a thing that has existence').
Attribute: describes the thing - the information about it that must be stored ('$40,000 describes that thing Homer Simpson').
Value: what an attribute takes on for one entity (25 for Age).
Domain (value set): the set of values the attribute can take, e.g. a Western student number over the domain of nine digits.

fields.Front: What is the difference between an entity type, an entity and an entity set?
fields.Back: Entity type: a set of entities with the same attributes - like a class. Entity (strictly): one INSTANCE of an entity type - like an object ('Homer would be an instance of the entity type student'). Entity set: the group of all entities of one type. Note: she usually says 'entity' for 'entity type'.

fields.Front: What are the domains of Age, Name and Cost on the slide?
fields.Back: Age: integers greater than 0 (notes say 0 to 120; in the video 0 to 114). Name: alphabetic characters/strings, possibly restricted in length. Cost: real numbers from 0.00 to some upper limit. A domain is more specific than a programming type: it is the values that make sense in the mini-world.

fields.Front: Define the three attribute pairs with their slide examples: composite/simple, multi-valued/single-valued, derived/stored.
fields.Back:
1. Composite can be divided into parts with independent meaning (Name = 'Bart Simpson' -> first, last); simple/atomic cannot (Age = 45).
2. Multi-valued holds several values for one entity (CollegeDegrees: a Master's and a PhD); single-valued exactly one (Age).
3. Derived can be computed from other stored data (Age); stored must be stored (Birthdate).

fields.Front: What are the two reasons an attribute value may be null? Give the slide examples and say why null is awkward.
fields.Back:
1. NOT APPLICABLE: Apartment Number - somebody lives in a house, so the value does not exist.
2. NOT KNOWN: Phone Number - everybody has one, but we do not know this person's.
Awkward because one symbol carries two meanings. Key attributes are never null (the blank OHIP number).

fields.Front: In Chen notation, how are these drawn: entity type, attribute, key attribute, multi-valued, composite, derived?
fields.Back:
Entity type: rectangle with the name inside.
Attribute: oval joined by a line to the entity.
Key attribute: oval with the name UNDERLINED ('key attributes are always underlined').
Multi-valued: DOUBLE oval.
Composite: oval with component ovals hanging off it.
Derived: DASHED oval.

fields.Front: APPLICATION: in 'each employee has a name, SSN, address, salary, sex and birth date', why is Employee an entity and Salary an attribute?
fields.Back: Employee is a thing that has existence (like Student, Classroom, Department), so it is an entity; Salary DESCRIBES an employee ($40,000 describes Homer Simpson), so it is an attribute. The test: does it have existence, or does it describe something?

fields.Front: APPLICATION: classify Birthdate, Age, Name(first, last), CollegeDegrees and SSN for an EMPLOYEE entity.
fields.Back: Birthdate: stored, simple, single-valued. Age: derived (from Birthdate). Name: composite. CollegeDegrees: multi-valued (double oval). SSN: key attribute (underlined). Store Birthdate, not Age.

fields.Front: In draw.io, which shapes does the instructor use for an entity, an ordinary attribute and a multi-valued attribute?
fields.Back: A plain RECTANGLE from the Entity Relation library area for the entity (the course uses Chen, not the newer style); the plain OVAL under General for ordinary attributes; the Entity Relation library's double-ring shape ONLY for multi-valued attributes such as Location. Underline a key with Text > Underline. Save early and after every stage.

fields.Text: When reading specs, {{c1::nouns}} are king: they usually become {{c1::entities or attributes}}, while {{c1::verbs}} become relationships.

A key attribute is one whose values are {{c1::unique}} for every entity, so it {{c1::identifies}} one entity - e.g. your {{c1::student number or Western user ID}}, or a patient's OHIP number. One is needed because there could be two students both named Homer Simpson; sometimes no single attribute is unique and you must combine attributes.

Store {{c1::Birthdate}} rather than {{c1::Age}}, because if you stored the latter you would have to {{c1::recalculate it}} every time it changed; a derived attribute is drawn only 'if you even want to show it'.

The test for whether an attribute is composite is whether there are {{c1::parts you might need to get at}} (e.g. just the first name); breaking a first name into {{c1::letters}} 'doesn't really make sense', so FirstName is {{c1::simple (atomic)}}.

'Most of the time entities don't have {{c1::two unique keys}}', but in the case study DEPARTMENT does: {{c1::Name and Number}}. The noun that is only implied in the specs is {{c1::date}} (when the employee started managing), which becomes StartDate on MANAGES.

Textbook (Elmasri §3.3.1): an entity is a thing with independent existence, and that existence may be {{c1::physical}} (a particular person, car, house or employee) or {{c1::conceptual}} (a company, a job, a university course).

Textbook (Elmasri §3.3.1): NULL has three meanings, not two - {{c1::not applicable}} (Apartment_number for a house); {{c1::unknown but known to exist}} (a person's Height); and {{c1::unknown whether it exists at all}} (a person's Home_phone: they may have no phone, or one we never collected).

Textbook (Elmasri §3.3.2): NOTATION - the ER model as Elmasri presents it has {{c1::no concept of a primary key}}; every key attribute is underlined separately and the primary key is chosen only during {{c1::the mapping to a relational schema}} (Chapter 9). A composite key must also be {{c1::minimal}}, with no superfluous attributes included.
